lesson.title: Bridging the Data Center and the Cloud
lesson.summary: Hybrid cloud networking connects an organization's on premises infrastructure with one or more cloud VPCs, usually over a VPN or a dedicated private connection, so the two environments function as one coherent network instead of two disconnected islands.
lesson.body:
Not every organization moves everything to the cloud at once, and some things may never move at all. Legacy systems that are expensive to rearchitect, equipment that must sit physically close to where it is used, regulatory requirements about where certain data can live, and plain cost considerations all mean that many real networks are a mix: some systems on premises, in a data center or server room the organization controls directly, and some systems running in one or more cloud VPCs. Hybrid cloud networking is the set of techniques for connecting those two worlds so that applications and data can move between them as needed, rather than living in two networks that cannot talk to each other at all.

There are two main ways to build that connection, and the choice comes down to a tradeoff between cost, setup speed, and consistency. The first is a site to site VPN, using exactly the VPN concepts covered earlier: an encrypted tunnel runs over the ordinary public internet between a router or firewall at the on premises site and a virtual private gateway attached to the cloud VPC. This is relatively cheap and can often be set up in a day, but because it rides over the public internet, its latency, jitter, and even availability are somewhat at the mercy of whatever congestion or outages happen to be affecting the internet at any given moment. The second option is a dedicated private connection, offered by every major cloud provider under names like Direct Connect, ExpressRoute, or Cloud Interconnect. This typically involves a physical or leased line running from the customer's facility, often by way of a colocation provider, directly into the cloud provider's network, entirely bypassing the public internet. It costs more and takes longer to provision, but delivers far more consistent latency, higher guaranteed throughput, and, at high enough data volumes, often lower cost per byte transferred.

Consider a hospital that keeps patient records on premises for compliance reasons, but wants to burst extra computing power into a cloud VPC during peak hours to run medical image analysis. Early on, while data volumes are modest and the project is still proving itself, a site to site VPN is a sensible choice: quick to set up, encrypted by default, and cheap to run. If the volume of image data being sent to the cloud grows large enough that internet variability starts causing real delays, or the cost of transferring that much data over a metered internet connection adds up, the hospital has a clear next step: move to a dedicated private connection for more predictable performance.

Once a hybrid connection exists, the two networks need a way to learn about each other's routes, and this is commonly handled with BGP, the same border gateway protocol used to exchange routing information across the internet at large. Running BGP between the on premises router and the cloud gateway lets each side automatically learn which address ranges live on the other side, and lets the connection fail over to a backup path automatically if the primary one goes down, rather than requiring someone to manually update routing tables every time something changes.

A well built hybrid connection is rarely a single link. Organizations commonly run two VPN tunnels, or two dedicated connections through different providers or paths, in an active and backup configuration, so a single failure does not sever the connection between environments entirely. Just as important is address planning: on premises subnets and cloud VPC subnets must not overlap, or routing between them becomes ambiguous, which means the CIDR planning you learned for a single VPC has to extend across the whole hybrid environment from the start, not be patched in after the fact.
